title: Life everlasting
hookLine: heaven, hell, purgatory: traditions differ, but all hope in God's mercy

cards: Norwich, England, May 1373. A woman of thirty, her name unknown, is so sick her priest is called to her bedside. He holds a crucifix before her eyes.
Over the next hours, she sees visions. She recovers, and later lives as an anchoress, walled into a small room beside the church of Saint Julian; tradition gives her its name: Julian of Norwich.
In what she writes down, she asks God her hardest question: why sin, why so much pain? The answer she hears is still quoted today. She's the guide to today's word, the creed's last line.

teach.h: ZOE AIONIOS: LIFE OF THE AGE.
teach.b: The creed ends: and the life everlasting. In John, the Greek is zoe aionios: the life of the age to come. It's not just more time, an endless Tuesday.
It's a different kind of life, God's own life, which John says can begin now.

John 3:16 is about it: "For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son, that whosoever believeth in him should not perish, but have everlasting life." After death? Here the churches honestly differ.
They speak of heaven: being with God, seeing God face to face. Church teaching also speaks of hell: the real possibility of refusing God, and being separated from God.

teach.h: THE CHURCHES DIFFER, AND SAY SO.
teach.b: Some understand it as endless; some Christians hope that in the end even hell may be emptied, though that hope isn't the official teaching of the large churches.
Fear of hell weighs on some people for years, sometimes even after they've stopped believing.
If that's you, it's worth telling someone you trust, a pastor, a counselor or a doctor; and if you ever feel in danger, in the US you can call or text 988, or reach local emergency help.
Catholics speak of purgatory: a purifying after death for those on their way to God. Orthodox Christians pray for the dead without defining purgatory, and Protestant churches generally don't hold it.
But under all of it runs one hope: God's mercy.
Julian heard it, in the old translation: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well."

teach.h: GOD SHALL WIPE AWAY ALL TEARS FROM THEIR EYES.
teach.b: Revelation pictures the end alike: "God shall wipe away all tears from their eyes; and there shall be no more death." That closes this part of the path: the creed, line by line, from I believe to life everlasting.

how: Christians say "and the life everlasting" at the end of the Apostles' Creed, pray at funerals in the hope of eternal life, and Catholics, with some Anglicans and Lutherans, remember the dead on All Souls' Day, November 2.

o: living on and on forever in this same world
the soul's long rest after the body dies
the life of the age to come, God's own life

games.q: what's inside the line — tap the pairs.
p: life of the age to come

s: in John, everlasting life only begins after death
John says the life of the age to come can begin now.
Catholics do; Orthodox pray for the dead without defining it; Protestant churches generally don't hold it.
Julian's best-known line came as an answer to her hardest question
she asked why there is sin and pain, and heard: all shall be well.

games.q: you're Julian, recovering from your visions. you ask God your hardest question: why is there sin and so much pain? what answer does she write down?
o: all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well.
games.why: Julian heard: "all shall be well, and all shall be well, and all manner of thing shall be well."

practice: Hold in hope someone you worry about, someone who has died, someone who seems lost, or yourself, without deciding what happens to them; that isn't yours to settle. Let Julian's words go round slowly: all shall be well.
If you pray, entrust them to God's mercy; if you don't, simply hold them, and hope.

wordCard.voice: Life everlasting. The life of the age to come, God's own life, which Christians say mercy opens.

orig.note: Greek: of the age, age-long. In zoe aionios: the life of the age to come.

carryVoice: Your line: mercy has the last word. The creed ends in hope. See you tomorrow.
